text:
The aspect of the countryside around Rome has something singularly remarkable about it: it is doubtless a desert, for there are neither trees nor dwellings; but the earth is covered with wild plants, ceaselessly renewed by the vigor of vegetation. These parasitic plants creep into the tombs, adorn the ruins, and seem to be there only to honor the dead. One would say that proud nature has rejected all the works of man since the Cincinnatuses ceased to guide the plow that furrowed her bosom; she produces plants at random, without allowing the living to make use of her wealth. These uncultivated plains must displease farmers, administrators, all those who speculate upon the land and wish to exploit it for the needs of man; but dreamy souls, occupied with death as much as with life, delight in contemplating this countryside of Rome, upon which the present time has left no trace; this earth that cherishes its dead and lovingly covers them with useless flowers, with useless plants that trail along the ground and never rise high enough to separate themselves from the ashes they appear to caress.

Oswald agreed that in this place one must experience more tranquillity than anywhere else. The soul does not suffer there as much from the images that grief presents to it; it seems that one still shares with those who are no more the charms of this air, this sun, and this greenery. Corinne observed the impression lord Nelvil was receiving from it, and conceived some hope from it. She did not flatter herself that she could console Oswald; she would not even have wished to efface from his heart the rightful regrets he owed to the loss of his father; but in the very feeling of regret there is something sweet and harmonious that one must endeavor to make known to those who have so far experienced only its bitterness: that is the only good one can do them.

“Let us stop here,” said Corinne, “facing this tomb, the only one that still remains almost intact: it is not the tomb of a famous Roman; it is that of Cecilia Metella, a young woman for whom her father had this monument erected.—Happy,” said Oswald, “happy are the children who die in their father’s arms, and who receive death in the bosom that gave them life! Death itself then loses its sting for them.”

“Yes,” said Corinne with emotion, “happy are those who are not orphans! Look, weapons have been carved upon this tomb, although it is that of a woman; but the daughters of heroes may have the trophies of their father upon their graves: the union of innocence and valor is a beautiful one. There is an elegy by Propertius that portrays, better than any other work of antiquity, this dignity of women among the Romans, more imposing and purer than even the splendor they enjoyed during the age of chivalry. Cornelia, who died in her youth, addresses the most touching farewells and consolations to her husband, and in it one feels, in almost every word, all that is worthy of respect and sacred in family bonds. The noble pride of a spotless life is portrayed in that majestic poetry of the Latins, in that poetry noble and austere like the masters of the world. ‘Yes,’ says Cornelia, ‘no stain has sullied my life: from the nuptial rite to the funeral pyre, I lived pure between the two torches.’ What an admirable expression!” exclaimed Corinne; “what a sublime image! And how enviable is the fate of the woman who can thus preserve the most perfect unity in her destiny, and carry but one memory to the grave! That is enough for a lifetime.”

As she finished these words, Corinne’s eyes filled with tears; a cruel feeling, a painful suspicion, took possession of Oswald’s heart. “Corinne,” he exclaimed, “Corinne! Has your delicate soul nothing with which to reproach itself? If I could dispose of myself, if I could offer myself to you, would I have no rivals in the past? Could I be proud of my choice? Would cruel jealousy not disturb my happiness?—I am free, and I love you as I have never loved before,” Corinne replied; “what more do you want? Must I be condemned to confess to you that, before I knew you, my imagination may have deceived me concerning the interest someone inspired in me! And is there not in the heart of man a divine pity for the errors that feeling, or at least the illusion of feeling, might have caused one to commit!” As she finished these words, a modest blush covered her face. Oswald shuddered, but remained silent. There was in Corinne’s gaze an expression of repentance and timidity that did not permit him to judge her harshly, and it seemed to him that a ray from heaven descended upon her to absolve her. He took her hand, pressed it against his heart, and knelt before her, uttering nothing, promising nothing, but contemplating her with a look of love that left room for every hope.

“Believe me,” Corinne said to lord Nelvil, “let us make no plans for the years to come: the happiest moments of life are still those that a benevolent chance grants us. Is it here, then, is it in the midst of tombs, that we should place so much faith in the future?—No,” exclaimed lord Nelvil, “no, I do not believe in the future that would separate us! These four days of absence have taught me all too well that I now exist only through you.” Corinne made no reply to these tender words, but devoutly gathered them into her heart; she was always afraid that, by prolonging the conversation about the feeling that alone occupied her, she might incite Oswald to declare his plans before longer habit had made separation impossible for him. Often, indeed, she deliberately directed his attention toward external objects; like that sultana of the Arabian tales who sought, through a thousand different stories, to captivate the interest of the man she loved, so as to postpone the decision of her fate until the moment when the charms of her mind won the victory.


CHAPTER II

Not far from the Appian Way, Oswald and Corinne had themselves shown the columbaria, where slaves are reunited with their masters, where one sees within a single tomb all those who lived under the protection of a single man or woman. Livia’s women, for example, those who, once devoted to the care of her beauty, struggled on her behalf against time and contested with the years for some of her charms, are placed beside her in small urns. One seems to see a collection of obscure dead surrounding an illustrious dead person, no less silent than the retinue. A short distance from there, one perceives a field where Vestal Virgins unfaithful to their vows were buried alive: a singular example of fanaticism in a naturally tolerant religion.

“I shall not take you to the catacombs,” Corinne said to lord Nelvil, “although, by a singular chance, they lie beneath this Appian Way, so that tombs rest upon tombs. But this refuge of persecuted Christians has something so dark and so terrible about it that I cannot bring myself to return there: it is not that touching melancholy one breathes in open places; it is the dungeon beside the sepulcher, the torment of life alongside the horrors of death. Doubtless one feels filled with admiration for the men who, through the sole power of enthusiasm, were able to endure this subterranean life and thus separated themselves entirely from the sun and from nature; but the soul is so ill at ease in that place that no good can result from it. Man is a part of creation; he must find his moral harmony in the whole of the universe, in the customary order of destiny; and certain violent and dreadful exceptions may astonish the mind, but they so greatly frighten the imagination that the soul’s habitual disposition cannot benefit from them. Let us go instead,” Corinne continued, “to see the Pyramid of Cestius: the Protestants who die here are all buried around that pyramid, and it is a gentle, tolerant, and liberal refuge.—Yes,” Oswald replied, “it is there that several of my compatriots have found their final resting place. Let us go there; perhaps that, at least, is how I shall never leave you.” Corinne shuddered at these words, and her hand trembled as she leaned upon lord Nelvil’s arm. “I am better,” he resumed, “much better since I have known you.” And Corinne’s face was once more illuminated by that sweet and tender joy, its habitual expression.
